articles.title: Israel piles pressure on Arab parties as Netanyahu seeks government
articles.summary: Israeli left-wing activists in Tel Aviv hold placards during a protest calling for a formation of a government together with Arab parties (Ilia YEFIMOVICH) Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's bloc on Thursday piled pressure on Israeli Arab leaders over unproven accusations of foreign funding, in a push to neuter parties that could hold the key to forming a government after an inconclusive election. Israeli President Isaac Herzog called for an investigation into allegations of fraud but cautioned against stigmatising the entire Arab Israeli community, who voted at unprecedented rates. Israel was nearing the completion of ballot-counting from Tuesday's election, in which neither Netanyahu nor the opposition bloc led by former military chief Gadi Eisenkot looked able to secure a majority in the parliament known as the Knesset. The Netanyahu camp's accusations, which a key Arab party has rejected, could bring uncertainty to the electoral process at a time when the threat of a return to war with Iran looms over the region. Israel's election saw soaring participation by Israeli Arabs, descendants of Palestinians who stayed after the country's creation in 1948, as outrage boiled at calls by officials such as National Security Minister Itamar Ben Gvir to treat their community much as Israel has dealt with Palestinians in Gaza and the occupied West Bank. Following Netanyahu's accusations of impropriety, Ben Gvir went so far as to encourage Israel to "immediately" order the arrests of Arab party leaders. Raam party leader Mansour Abbas said he welcomed an investigation into claims of wrongdoing, adding that his moderate Islamist party had "no connection" with the accusations. The Arab parties together have enough votes to take the opposition bloc over the finish line, but Eisenkot has baulked after relentless attacks by Netanyahu, who warned his right-wing Jewish base that voting for the opposition would put Arabs in power. - 'Political earthquake' - Supreme Court Justice Noam Sohlberg, a conservative who heads the Central Election Commission, requested an investigation by the Shin Bet security service into allegations that Raam received money from Qatar, the energy-rich Gulf powerbroker that has channels to Hamas. "The Raamgate scandal is a political earthquake. Israel's elections have been stolen!" Netanyahu's Likud party said. Government officials did not offer evidence to back the allegations, and left-wing candidate Yair Golan accused Netanyahu of attempting to stir controversy after failing to get a majority. "Now he is trying to challenge the election results through an ugly delegitimisation campaign against the will of the people, and against the Arab public in particular." Netanyahu himself has long been under the cloud of allegations related to Qatar after the arrests last year of two of his aides for allegedly receiving payments from the Gulf state. Netanyahu, Israel's longest-serving prime minister, for years tacitly supported Qatar funding for Hamas-ruled Gaza, hoping to preserve stability. That paradigm collapsed on October 7, 2023, when Hamas carried out the deadliest single attack ever on Israel under Netanyahu's watch. - Kingmakers under pressure - With nearly 93 percent of the vote counted, Netanyahu's bloc was at 53 seats and the opposition forces led by Eisenkot on 48 -- both well under the 61 needed to form a government. The two main Arab formations were on track for an unprecedented 19 seats between them. Some observers quickly said that the allegations would help Netanyahu by making the Arab lawmakers even more toxic to Eisenkot. Yousef Jabareen, the head of the leftist Arab-majority Joint List, told AFP on Wednesday that he was willing to cooperate with the opposition to bring down Netanyahu but without joining it in a government. In response to the new allegations, Eisenkot said he was receiving updates and promised "utmost vigilance" against election interference. "On the other hand, we cannot allow political actors to exploit the situation and influence the timing of the inauguration of the 26th Knesset," he said. One of Eisenkot's right-leaning allies, Avigdor Lieberman, called the allegations "dramatic and unprecedented" and urged a swift investigation. An Israeli police statement said that they would investigate every complaint about election integrity. - The great survivor - Netanyahu, who has led Israel on and off for more than 19 years, is known as a wily political operator. He tried on Tuesday to raise allegations of fraud, saying that Arab parties were caught with envelopes of cash, and his Likud party peddled the accusations throughout Thursday. Police said they arrested three suspects but the election commission called it an isolated local case. Another factor that could play into the formation of a government is an attack on Iran. Netanyahu has repeatedly threatened to strike Iran, with his ally US President Donald Trump signalling he was ready to attack after next Tuesday's US midterm elections, in which his Republican Party is forecast to lose ground. Eisenkot has warned the military that Netanyahu has no mandate and that officers must put Israel's security over the premier's "political needs". An attack could raise pressure on Eisenkot to join an emergency unity government, an option he has publicly ruled out, or keep the clock running until Israel can call new elections. President Herzog will decide after the publication of the official results which person to task with a first chance of forming a government. sct/lba/smw/ser This article originally appeared on AFP at https://www.yahoo.com/news/politics/articles/israel-piles-pressure-arab-parties-094327123.html

articles.title: DoorDash acquires Instacart for $17 billion, doubling down on hyper-local delivery
articles.summary: DoorDash ( DASH ) announced plans to acquire hyper-local grocery delivery provider Instacart ( CART ) on Thursday morning in a deal valued at $17 billion. DoorDash, which is primarily known for its restaurant food delivery business, will pay $65 per Instacart share, a 26% premium over the stock’s Oct. 22 closing price. The transaction includes 75% cash, with Instacart stockholders able to elect cash, DoorDash stock, or a combination of both. Instacart's board of directors unanimously approved the deal, according to a press release. "Grocery is one of the hardest things to get right online,” DoorDash CEO Tony Xu said in the release. “Instacart has spent years learning to do that well for grocers, while DoorDash has built a delivery network and technology that local stores rely on every day. Together, we could give stores of every size more of those tools and unlock the potential of grocery delivery." DoorDash stock popped over 5% in premarket trading, while Instacart stock edged lower. The acquisition comes as Walmart  ( WMT ) and Amazon ( AMZN ) have been taking share of the grocery delivery market, especially for same-day and one-hour delivery. Prior to the announcement, Wedbush analyst Ygal Arounian said the combination of Instacart and DoorDash could "potentially prove to be a competitive differentiation." "A combination of strong restaurant delivery plus a marketplace including various grocers from Instacart can be a critical combination against Walmart and Amazon in particular, who continue to push in this market as well," Arounian said. Walmart currently holds roughly a 30.9% share of online grocery, ahead of Amazon at roughly 23.6%, per Wedbush. For customers worried about what the Instacart acquisition means for prices, the company said shoppers will now get two memberships for the price of one and more choices. "Instacart customers could shop at more than 50,000 additional stores, on top of the nearly 100,000 stores on the Instacart platform today," the release said. For local business owners, the company said this would allow them more ways to earn. Miami Beach, Florida,Door dash delivery, adult courier turning back smiling. articles.title: The Fed held rates steady, but your savings and debt could still feel the impact
articles.summary: The Federal Reserve left short-term interest rates unchanged on Wednesday, following September's first hike in more than three years. Based on 30-day fed funds futures prices , Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh and the Federal Open Market Committee are likely to raise the benchmark interest rate by a quarter-point in December. "The Federal Reserve's interest rate decision takes center stage this week after a hotter-than-expected September CPI report showed price pressures broadening," Ehsan Khoman, economist with the BlackRock Investment Institute, said in an analysis. "We don't view recent tightening as the start of a sustained hiking cycle." What will a higher rate environment mean for your money? The federal funds rate influences not only the stock market, but also savings rates, interest charges, and, to a lesser degree, mortgage rates. Here's how to prepare for the impact on your deposits, credit, and debt. » Fed meeting live updates: Interest rates held steady in split vote ahead of midterm elections How a Fed rate hike affects checking and savings accounts A series of Fed rate hikes will likely slowly lift deposit earnings. However, deposit accounts are mostly for convenience, not substantial returns. So far in 2026, the gains have been meager. Checking accounts Your checking account churns cash flow to pay bills. The liquidity limits your earning power. The national average interest rate on checking accounts has barely budged this year, remaining at 0.07%. A Fed short-term interest rate increase may nudge earnings incrementally higher. Savings accounts Interest rates on savings accounts are only marginally better, clinging to 0.38%. But savings accounts are for near-term money. High-yield savings accounts have been more effective at paying interest. Rates are split in the 3% to 4% range. This is one category where rate shopping and subsequent increases in the Fed rate really pay off. Money market accounts If you have $10,000 or more that you want to keep on the sidelines but easy to tap when you need it, money market accounts have been convenient — but low-paying, with a national average payout of only 0.63%. A high-yield money market account is a better option, where you may still find a rate just under 4%, but mostly in the mid-3% range. What a rate hike does to CDs CD rates have begun inching higher. The national average on a 12-month CD is 1.76%, but you can find better deals if you're willing to shop around — and move your money to the best offer. Your minimum deposit and term will affect your rate. Fed rate hikes may ultimately sweeten CD rates. What a rate hike will mean for mortgages And then there are mortgage rates , often the largest borrowing expense consumers face. Fed interest rate increases don't usually affect mortgage rates — the bond market often prices in hikes before monetary policy moves. At the end of February and into early March, mortgage rates were hitting three-year lows. Then the war in the Middle East began, and rather than falling further, home loan rates reversed course and edged higher. Home loan rates have recently topped 7% (depending on the rate reporting source), mirroring the higher yields of the 10-year Treasury note . Housing industry analysts at the Mortgage Bankers Association and Fannie Mae predict that mortgage rates will remain near 7.5% through 2027. What a rate hike means for personal loans and student loans Personal loans Personal loan interest rates have risen slightly to an average of 11.9%. Advertised personal loan rates vary widely, from 6% to 9%. The Federal Reserve influences consumer loan rates by setting the federal funds rate, which affects how much banks charge each other for overnight lending. That cost typically gets passed on to borrowers through higher or lower rates on personal, auto, and student loans. Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh delivers a speech on the day of his swearing-in ceremony at the White House in Washington, D.C. REUTERS / REUTERS Student loans The Federal Reserve doesn't set student loan rates directly, but its federal funds rate influences the 10-year Treasury yield (which determines federal loan rates) and the prime rate (which determines private loan rates). The federal funds rate doesn't directly determine federal student loan interest rates, but it can influence them indirectly. Congress sets the federal student loan rates based on the 10-year Treasury note, adding a fixed margin each year. But the 10-year Treasury yield moves with investor demand, not the Fed's rate. When investors expect high inflation or strong economic growth, they demand higher yields, which can push federal student loan rates higher. That said, if the Fed's rate hikes successfully cool inflation, Treasury yields may drop — and the following year's federal student loan rates could be lower. Private student loans are offered by banks, credit unions, and online lenders, many of which use the prime rate as a basis for setting their interest rates. The prime rate moves alongside the Federal Reserve's rate decisions. So, when the Fed raises rates, new private loan rates usually rise, and when it cuts rates, they tend to fall. What happens to credit cards when the Fed raises rates Credit card interest affects everyone — except those who pay off their balance each month. Rates have climbed from around 16% in 2021 to an average of over 22% toda Michele Raneri, vice president and head of U.S. research at TransUnion, expects consumers to see "minimally higher" borrowing costs as variable-rate credit products reflect the Fed's interest rate hike. "A consumer carrying the average Q2 2026 credit card balance of $6,610 at a 22% APR could see an increase of $1.38 in minimum monthly payments as those higher rates are passed on," Raneri said in a statement. "While the near-term impact on minimum monthly credit card payments may be relatively small, higher borrowing costs can add up over time, particularly for consumers carrying larger balances or making only minimum payments. Reducing revolving debt will limit the impact of rising interest rates, she added. Yahoo Finance tip: The best way to earn a lower credit card interest rate right away is to ask. If you make regular payments and have seen your credit score improving, it's a good time to call your credit card provider and ask for a lower interest rate. Yahoo Personal Finance How the Fed's interest rate policy impacts your investments "There's an old Wall Street adage that says, 'Don't fight the Fed,'" Kevin Gordon, head of macro research and strategy at Schwab, said in an analysis. "The idea behind it was that there's often a lot of turbulence associated with Fed rate-hiking cycles." He noted that history shows an average maximum loss of more than 10% for the S&P 500 sometime within 12 months after the start of a higher-interest-rate cycle. "Broadly, though, we would say that the economic backdrop is still relatively favorable for the Fed to be hiking. So even if it is a hiking cycle where they do hike more than once, we think that the economy can probably hold up," he added. Stock prices often react to the Fed's rate actions, but they are only one of many factors affecting the investing climate and stock prices. AI investments and oil-price-fueled inflation seem to be the most motivating factors for equity markets these days. If you want to manage your investments for the current environment, monitor broader economic and corporate profit trends, as well as interest rates. If you prefer to stay conservative, fill your portfolio with high-quality stocks that have proven themselves in all economic cycles. Then, wait patiently for long-term growth. articles.title: Alaska election officials oppose DOJ's involvement in Senate race
articles.summary: From left: Daniel J. Sullivan Jr., Mary Peltola and incumbent Sen. Dan S. Sullivan. - AP/Getty Images/Reuters Alaska officials said new revelations in The New York Times about efforts by Democrats to recruit a Senate candidate with the same name as GOP incumbent Sen. Dan S. Sullivan do not change the state’s opposition to a Trump administration lawsuit seeking to potentially delay certification of the election. The Times story , a spokesperson for the Alaska Department of Law told CNN in an email, confirms the “initial concerns” election officials had about the candidacy of Daniel J. Sullivan, a retired teacher, but it has “no impact on the current litigation.” “Placing candidates on the ballot is a matter of state law, not federal law,” said spokesperson Sam Curtis, noting that the Alaska Supreme Court has already decided that Daniel J. Sullivan would be on the ballot. The Justice Department, meanwhile, is citing a federal law in the case that “does not dictate what candidates can run in elections and does not authorize the relief the DOJ seeks,” Curtis said. “The Division is bound by the Alaska Supreme Court’s order and is committed to running a fair election and assisting voters as needed,” Curtis said. The story published Wednesday rattled one of the country’s most competitive Senate races with less than a week until Election Day. Mary Peltola, the state’s former at-large House member, is considered one of Senate Democrats’ top recruits of the midterms and her campaign continues to deny any involvement in Daniel J. Sullivan’s campaign. Republicans have been concerned enough about the race that both President Donald Trump and Vice President JD Vance have made trips to Alaska in recent weeks. Trump, who has complained about the two Sullivan issue for months and said he directed the Justice Department lawsuit last week, piled on with multiple social media posts slamming Peltola over the story, including one that said she “should be removed from the Ballot and prosecuted.” “So should the FAKE Dan Sullivan,” Trump wrote on Truth Social. “Nothing else will do!” The incumbent’s campaign accused Peltola in a statement of spending months “gaslighting Alaskans.” “I am pressing my opponent to come clean,” Sullivan said while speaking with Fox News’ Sean Hannity Wednesday night. “She’s been lying for over a year. She’s run a campaign about supposed corruption. She’s the corrupt one working with DC insiders to trick Alaskans. So what we’re going to do is we’re going to make sure every single Alaskan knows about this.” Attorney General Todd Blanche on Fox News touted the Times’ story as proof that the Justice Department was right in bringing its unprecedented federal lawsuit. But when pressed over whether anything illegal had occurred that gives the DOJ the ability to intervene in the election, which is run by states, Blanche could not say. The Justice Department on Wednesday told a federal judge it would like to seek answers and evidence from Peltola’s campaign regarding the Times report and Sullivan issue, which it called a “conspiracy.” Late Wednesday, Alaska’s Republican Gov. Mike Dunleavy also said he was ordering an investigation into whether criminal charges or civil action should be brought over the alleged Democratic efforts to confuse voters. “Deliberately tricking voters into casting their ballots for someone else strikes at the integrity of our elections,” he said on X . “Anyone or any organization found to have broken the law must be held accountable.” Some Democrats noted that Republicans have also meddled in the race to boost spoiler candidates. An array of GOP groups, for example, contributed to a super PAC that attacked Peltola in the primary and promoted a lesser-known Democratic candidate and a Green Party candidate. “This is basically a more extreme version of what the parties do all the time, which is try to find a candidate on the other side who can siphon votes away from the major party competitor,” election law specialist Rick Hasen told CNN. “And, you know, you can’t really hold someone responsible for impure motives.” Dean Franita Tolson of the University of Southern California Gould School of Law said the Times reporting doesn’t give the Department of Justice’s lawsuit any more credence. “At the end of the day, the federal government should not try to block certification of a race because they don’t like the outcome,” she said. “It, I think, makes the Peltola campaign look bad,” Derek Muller, a law professor at the University of Notre Dame Law School, added. “I think it will adversely affect her in the eyes of some voters, but from litigation perspective, I think it really won’t affect things at this stage.” This story has been updated with additional information. articles.title: Details of thousands of U.S. immigration agents leaked in a massive hack
articles.summary: US immigration agents often work with their faces covered and do not wear identification. [Reuters] Details of more than 41,000 personnel working for the US Department of Homeland Security (DHS), including thousands involved in immigration enforcement, have been leaked to the public. The leak includes names, work addresses and phone numbers of DHS staff, including agents working with Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and Customs and Border Protection, along with descriptions of the work they do for each agency. Wednesday's leak marks the third time in recent weeks that a government agency has been targeted by leaks or hacks. A DHS spokesperson said the agency is "aware of a potential breach and is actively working to address the situation swiftly and effectively." "We take all security threats against our employees and officers seriously and will work to ensure all are properly protected," the spokesperson added. "We will update the public when more information is available." The seemingly unprecedented breach of employee information was made public online. A group called the Department of Peace accessed the information from DHS, while journalist and cybersecurity researcher maia crimew alongside the website Distributed Denial of Secrets put it online. The information was put in a database named Icepick. Most of the agents included, more than 21,000 of them, work for CBP, according to the data. Nearly 6,600 work for ICE. Other records show agents with Homeland Security Investigations, the Federal Protective Service and even people working for the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency. The leaked information also included dozens of previously unknown operation names, the agents that led and worked on those operations, and some of the technology they used in their work, including tech provided by Cellbrite and Palantir. The groups wrote in an online statement that the the leak was not meant to be a directory of every DHS agent. Rather the aim was to replace "anonymity with accountability", according to Emma Best, a co founder of DDoSecrets. "The leak is extraordinary but deceptive in its simplicity as it identifies the officials responsible for overseeing covert and undercover operations, the government's hunt for leakers and the failed BlueLeaks investigation - along with key personnel in DHS's ever-escalating rendition and deportation programs," Best added. BlueLeaks refers to a massive leak of US police data in 2020, data from which DDoSecrets also hosted. A spokesperson for the Department of Peace pointed directly at actions by ICE agents for the group's work to hack DHS records. "On July 17th, Markwayne Mullin said he was 'turning up the heat'. This is what happens to ICE when you do that," the spokesperson wrote on Wednesday. Mullin in March became Secretary of Homeland Security. The Department of Peace said it accessed the DHS agent profiles through a single sign-on service called Okta. Okta is a popular online security tool that organisations use to ensure that only people with access to internal platforms are logging on to them. A spokeswoman for Okta said the company is aware of the claims being made, but said: "Okta is secure, and we have no evidence our data or systems were compromised." Last month, the FBI was hacked by a group called ShinyHunters, which took personal information about thousands of agents. In recent days, the Federal Election Commission, which makes public political campaign donation data, was taken offline because of a suspected hacking attempt. Public backlash to US immigration enforcement has been building as the Trump Administration has pushed a huge increase in arrests and deportations of people suspected of being in the country illegally. Immigration operations this year have repeatedly turned violent , with ICE agents shooting at more than two dozen people and killing at least nine people. Those killings include the high profile deaths of Alex Pretti and Renee Good, both of whom were shot and killed by ICE agents this year in Minnesota, despite not being the targets of arrests. Often, ICE agents carry out enforcement actions while their faces are covered by masks and sunglasses. Immigration agents rarely identify themselves, despite being required by law to do so, and US politicians have publicly demanded DHS enforces the requirement. Since President Donald Trump returned to office in 2025, the US has enacted nearly 1 million deportations , according to data from the Migration Policy Institute. More than 70% of the deportations have been of people with no criminal record. articles.title: Trump and Obama trade personal jabs as their midterm rivalry heats up
articles.summary: By Bo Erickson and Nandita Bose CHILLICOTHE, Ohio/MORROW, Georgia, Oct 28 (Reuters) - Neither man is on the ballot but Republican President Donald Trump and Democratic former President Barack Obama took prominent roles on the campaign trail on Wednesday, with less than a week to go before congressional races that could shift the balance of power in Washington. While Trump has been on a weeks-long campaign blitz that ‌has underlined Republican concerns about losing control of Congress for the final two years of his presidency, Obama had kept a relatively low public profile until the past week, during which he has delivered blistering ‌speeches criticizing Trump. Thirty-five of the 100 Senate seats and all 435 seats in the House of Representatives are being contested next Tuesday. Nonpartisan analysts generally favor Democrats' chances of capturing a majority in the House, with the contest for the Senate seen as very close. On Wednesday, Obama appeared ​in Morrow, Georgia, near Atlanta, where he urged voters to support Democratic Senator Jon Ossoff, who faces a challenge from Representative Mike Collins, a Republican. While delivering the standard Democratic critique of Trump for imposing tariffs and going to war in Iran, Obama also said America's values were on the ballot, as he recalled the vision of slain civil rights leader Martin Luther King Jr., who is buried in Atlanta. "There is a moral component to the choices we face right now," Obama said. "We are not going to fix the system that's broken, we're not going to unrig our economy, so long as we've got a culture where anything goes, where people in the highest offices of the land think it's OK to lie and cheat and bully, ‌if we continue to have a culture where money is deemed the only measure ⁠of our worth," Obama said. Trump's public approval rating has fallen to a near record low, with Americans increasingly sour on the high cost of living and the Iran war, but he remains an animating force in the party and has campaigned hard to increase Republican turnout. Americans have been voting for weeks, with 40 million ballots already cast, according to the University of Florida's ⁠Election Lab. A total of 45.9 million Americans voted early in the last midterm elections in 2022. Addressing a rally inside a modest college gymnasium in the Ohio town of Chillicothe, the president appeared with Senator Jon Husted of Ohio as he faces a challenge from Democratic former Senator Sherrod Brown. Trump attacked Brown for supporting immigration policies the president said had overwhelmed Springfield, Ohio, with Haitian migrants. "The town went to hell," he said. Trump spread false claims during the 2024 presidential campaign that Haitian immigrants in Springfield were eating cats and dogs, allegations local ​officials ​repeatedly said were untrue. TRUMP FACES PROTESTERS Enthusiastic crowds have cheered Trump at rallies throughout the campaign, but hundreds of protesters lined Trump's motorcade ​route in rural Chillicothe, raising banners that read, "Republican against Trump," "Grab them by the ballot" and “GOP: Guardians ‌of pedophiles." During the rally, protesters interrupted Trump several times, including at least one who shouted about deceased convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein. "I threw Jeffrey Epstein the hell out of Mar-a-Lago," Trump said in response. Trump and Epstein socialized in the 1990s and early 2000s, but Trump has said they later had a falling out and that he barred Epstein from Mar-a-Lago, Trump's private club in Palm Beach, Florida. Justice Department releases from the Epstein files have included references to Trump, as well as many other prominent figures. The department has cautioned that some materials contain allegations that were unverified or uncorroborated. Protesters have interrupted Trump at virtually all his recent rallies. He typically accuses them of being paid protesters as they are carted off by security. In Cleveland on Saturday, Obama poked fun at Trump's taste in interior decorating, saying, "He's got the White House looking like Saddam Hussein opened a Cheesecake Factory," a chain of casual dining restaurants. Trump defended his White House decor and said ‌Obama left the property deteriorated. "The White House, I think, is the number one symbol of our country, and we can't have a ​White House with broken windows, with broken stone that hasn't been painted in 30 years," Trump said in Ohio. ALASKA, MICHIGAN RACES Democrats will need ​to pick up seats in traditionally Republican-leaning states such as Ohio, Iowa or Alaska to overcome the current ​53-47 Republican majority in the Senate. The New York Times reported that aides to Mary Peltola, the Senate Democratic nominee in Alaska, worked with the campaign's lawyers and senior staff at Senate Democrats’ ‌campaign arm to recruit two candidates who are on the ballot and could siphon votes ​from incumbent Republican US Senator Dan Sullivan. Representatives for Peltola did ​not immediately respond to requests for comment. "Mary Peltola should resign from the race. I think she should be criminally prosecuted for what she did," Trump told reporters before departing for Ohio. In Michigan, where Republican Mike Rogers and Democrat Abdul El-Sayed are locked in a tight race for the Senate seat being vacated by Democratic Senator Gary Peters, both campaigns are relying on high-profile allies to energize supporters and boost turnout. Rogers spent the ​day campaigning with Senator Ted Cruz of Texas on a four-stop bus tour culminating ‌in Imlay City, a small community northeast of Detroit. El-Sayed, meanwhile, was scheduled to join Peters and fellow Michigan Senator Elissa Slotkin for an evening canvassing rally in Downriver, southwest of Detroit. articles.title: Hegseth fires Pentagon's top military planner as Trump weighs new strikes on Iran
articles.summary: WASHINGTON (AP) — Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has fired the Pentagon’s top military planner, a defense official said Wednesday, the latest in a series of generals to be ousted and one that comes even as President Donald Trump is weighing renewed strikes on Iran in the eight-month-long war. Army Lt. Gen. Brett Sylvia was removed as head of strategy, plans and policy on the Joint Chiefs of Staff. He is the second general to be ousted from the post, known in military circles as the “J5,” under Hegseth. His predecessor, Lt. Gen. Joseph McGee, was forced to retire last October. The defense official, who spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss sensitive personnel matters, said there is no immediate replacement for Sylvia and no reason has been given for the firing. The move was reported earlier by The Atlantic. A spokesperson for the Joint Staff said “the Chairman, the Joint Staff, and the Joint Force extend our deepest gratitude to Lt. Gen. Brett Sylvia and his family for their 32 years of distinguished service to our nation” and they "wish him and his family the best.” Typically, the J5 director and their staff are responsible for generating and coordinating military plans with both the chairman of the Joint Chiefs and the president. Sylvia's firing comes as Trump has repeatedly floated starting new military operations against Iran. Trump has vowed to “finish the job” in Iran after launching the war with Israel eight months ago and said new strikes are an option after the midterm elections next week. U.S. officials have told several Middle East countries and regional allies to be prepared for potential renewed military action after Tuesday's elections as well as for the possibility that Iran will attempt to retaliate against them, two diplomats briefed on the matter said. They say Trump has not made a final decision on new strikes. A third U.S. aircraft carrier and thousands of additional troops are making their way to the region . Before arriving at the Joint Staff, Sylvia served as the commander of the 101st Airborne Division at Fort Campbell, Kentucky, until May 2025, according to his official biography, which has now been taken offline. He also previously served as the vice director for the J5. He is the latest in nearly two dozen generals, admirals and other military leaders to be fired, forced to retire or otherwise depart under Hegseth's tenure — almost all of which have not been publicly explained by the Pentagon. That includes the civilian secretaries of the Army and Navy as well as some top uniformed officers for the military services. The Pentagon did not immediately respond to messages seeking comment late Wednesday. Hegseth said last month that he ordered the military to double the cuts to the overall number of top officers to a 20% decrease to be completed by Jan. 1, 2027. There are currently roughly 800 flag and general officer positions. “I call it accountability and long overdue,” Hegseth told junior officers and enlisted leaders at the Marine Corps Base Quantico on Sept. 30. Some members of Congress have criticized cuts to the ranks of generals as a “purge” that will take years to rebuild. “He’s got some kind of like deep-seated grievance about leadership in the military,” Sen. Mark Kelly, D-Ariz., a former Navy combat pilot who has been critical of Hegseth, said last month. “He’s purging a generation of great leaders of the military, and it’s going to take a generation to recover from it.” ___ Associated Press writers Aamer Madhani in Washington and Samy Magdy in New York contributed to this report. articles.title: 2 right-wing provocateurs face election-related charges in Minnesota
articles.summary: Two right-wing provocateurs, James O'Keefe and Cam Higby, are facing election-related charges in Minnesota after posting videos of an undercover stunt intended to expose alleged deficiencies in election security . Hennepin County Attorney Mary Moriarty said each man faces a count of unlawful voting and identity theft. "Elections are the bedrock of democracy and their protection is one of our highest priorities," Moriarty said in a statement. "Individuals engaging in unlawful conduct related to our elections will be held accountable." Hegseth directs military cyber forces to use 'every authorized asset' to defend midterm elections from foreign interference amid Trump's funding cuts to election security agencies O'Keefe, a self-proclaimed "guerilla journalist" infamous for his undercover videos, and Higby, a social media influencer, posted the video at the heart of the charges in August. It shows the two men approaching election judges at multiple voting precincts in Minneapolis wearing burqas, speaking in fake accents, and allegedly misrepresenting their identities, in an effort to expose what O'Keefe and Higby say are gaps in the rules that allow residents to vouch for the identity of other voters. The video, which remains pinned on Higby's X account, is called "I Wore Burqa To EXPOSE Election FRAUD In Minneapolis." No ballots were cast in the course of their efforts. Prosecutors said Wednesday that O'Keefe and Higby deceived the election judges by using the identities of real Minnesota voters "without those voters' knowledge or permission" in violation of state law. Each count carries up to five years in prison and a fine of up to $10,000. Neither man is in custody, according to charging documents. Tim Evans/AFP via Getty Images - PHOTO: People fill their ballots during the first day of early voting for the midterm elections in Minneapolis, Minnesota, October 16, 2026. In a statement, O'Keefe called the charges "weaponized lawfare" and defended his undercover video as journalism protected by the Constitution. He vowed to fight the charges. "This is not political," he said. "It is fundamental. It is about whether citizens still have the right to question their government." In a post shared on X, Higby said, "No laws were broken. They want me in PRISON for exposing election vulnerabilities in their state." O'Keefe did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Steve Simon, the state's top election official, said in a statement that "any attempt to disrupt or deceive our election workers will not be tolerated." The charges announced Wednesday in Minnesota are not O'Keefe's first brush with the law. In 2010, O'Keefe pleaded guilty in Louisiana to a misdemeanor charge of entering a federal property under false pretenses after he posed as a telephone repairman to gain access to a U.S. senator's New Orleans office. articles.title: Manhunt grows for escaped killer who may have left area where truck was ditched
articles.summary: Jacob Morley, a convicted killer on the loose since Sunday, has no known connection to the small Illinois town where the truck he is accused of stealing was found, the police chief said Wednesday. “What we have seen kind of leads us in the direction that he’s not still here. But that doesn’t mean that we’ve stopped looking,” Marion Police Chief David Fitts said. Morley, 28, convicted of killing a co-worker in 2022 , was serving a life sentence when he escaped from Northwest Correctional Complex in Tiptonville, Tennessee, sometime before 11:30 p.m. Sunday, officials there said. Morley had stolen a work truck, and early Tuesday that truck was found behind a business in Marion, a town of around 16,000 that is around 100 miles north of Tiptonville, authorities in Marion and Tennessee said. Security video captured Morley driving away in a flatbed truck. There have been no reports in Marion of any other stolen vehicles, and there was no evidence around the truck that was found, Fitts said. There have also been no confirmed sightings, he said. “There’s really nowhere for him to go here where he wouldn’t be recognized. His face is all over the news,” Fitts said. Morley has no known connection to Marion or southern Illinois, he said. “Have no idea why he would come here, other than I-57 is a major interstate and it runs right through the middle of our town,” Fitts said. “And I don’t know, maybe he was low on gas and just pulled off. I don’t know.” Morley was convicted of first-degree murder, abuse of a corpse, tampering with evidence and aggravated burglary after a trial in February 2025. He also pleaded guilty to theft of property. He was accused of shooting Cody Birchfield in the back of the head in 2022, according to court documents. Birchfield’s body was found in a large metal box under Morley’s residence, the documents say. Birchfield’s sister, Carrie Norman, said Wednesday that “it feels like a scary movie.” The family, she said, “have to go back through the experience — once again. Once again, because you don’t know where he’s at, but you know what he’s capable of.” Also Wednesday, the reward for information leading to Morley’s arrest increased from $2,500 to $15,000, a combined sum from the Tennessee governor’s office, the Tennessee Bureau of Investigation and the U.S. Marshals Service, the bureau said. Fitts said he wished Morley had been caught, but he urged people not to take things into their own hands. “This is really frustrating that we can’t find him. Somebody will eventually, I have no doubt in my mind. I wish it was us so we could catch him now,” Fitts said. “But, and I just want to let our people know that, again, don’t approach him. Call 911. We’ll handle it.” Around 11:30 p.m. Sunday, prison staff members confirmed that Morley was unaccounted for and conducted an emergency count and search of the facility, the Tennessee Department of Correction said. Security video showed Morley “breached the perimeter fence and exited the facility in his TDOC uniform,” the department said. The department has not given more details about how the escape occurred, which it said Wednesday is under investigation. articles.title: Judge denies feds' request to block 20,000 California ballots in blistering opinion
articles.summary: A sign points toward voting stations inside the Arroyo Seco Regional Branch Library in Los Angeles. (Ronaldo Bolanos / Los Angeles Times) A federal judge in a blistering opinion Wednesday denied a Trump administration request to immediately block California elections officials from counting the ballots of 20,000 voters whose citizenship the administration questions. The administration swiftly said it would appeal. U.S. District Judge David O. Carter ruled that the administration’s allegations were “not credible” and that the intervention it sought would violate a host of federal laws, sow chaos in the ongoing midterm election, likely lead to the disenfranchisement of legitimate voters and foster future political meddling in elections. “This request violates longstanding constitutional principles mandating that states have control over their elections,” Carter wrote. “If [the Trump administration’s] last-minute request for relief were granted, either party could create chaos for their own political purposes to disrupt the election process.” Carter, an appointee of President Clinton, wrote that never in American history “has the federal government, on the eve of an election, sought to coerce a state and local government to abandon their own Constitutional elections procedures and bend to the will of the Executive Branch,” and that, in bringing its suit, the Trump administration was asking the court to “believe that it reigns as a sole sovereign.” “But California and its people are sovereign, too,” Carter wrote. Carter’s ruling was the second to deny the Trump administration a temporary restraining order against the state and Los Angeles County this week, after a three-judge panel of the U.S. 9th Circuit Court of Appeals denied the government’s emergency request in a separate order Monday. Carter ruled after a 3½-hour hearing Tuesday, where a slew of attorneys for the state, county and independent voting rights groups argued against the administration’s demands. Read more: Your last-minute voter guide to California's 2026 general election First Assistant U.S. Atty. Bill Essayli — who is the top federal prosecutor in L.A. and argued for the Trump administration at Tuesday’s hearing — wrote on X that his office had already filed notice of appeal and “will immediately seek an emergency order” reversing Carter back in the 9th Circuit. “Every day, more ballots are processed by election officials. This ongoing emergency disenfranchises American citizens through dilution,” Essayli wrote. State elections officials, other state leaders, voting rights advocates and election experts all cheered the ruling. “For the second day this week, our country’s legal system is standing up to the President’s authoritarian attempts to remain in power unchecked and unchallenged,” Gov. Gavin Newsom said. “Today’s ruling is yet another important victory for the rule of law and the right to vote,” said California Atty. Gen. Rob Bonta. “But this fight is not over. We will keep fighting to protect California’s elections from unlawful federal interference and get this baseless lawsuit dismissed.” Los Angeles County Registrar-Recorder/County Clerk Dean Logan, whom the Trump administration sued along with the state and Secretary of State Shirley Weber, said the ruling “reinforces what we have maintained throughout this process: election integrity and the protection of eligible voters go hand in hand.” Anna Baldwin, the director of voting rights litigation at Campaign Legal Center who argued before Carter on behalf of the NAACP and the League of United Latin American Citizens, said Carter had “affirmed what the Constitution has already made clear: The states and Congress oversee our elections, not the White House and not the Department of Justice.” Read more: Read the ballot ruling Rick Hasen, director of the Safeguarding Democracy Project at UCLA School of Law, said Carter’s ruling was as sweeping a rejection of the Trump administration’s illegitimate attempts to interfere in California’s election as could possibly be written. “The federal government lost in every way it could possibly lose. It lost on the law, and it lost on the facts, and it lost on the equities — [or] weighing the harms to the various parties,” Hasen said. And that is appropriate given that the case was a “total overreach of federal power,” Hasen said. “The Constitution’s clear that states have the authority to run Congressional elections unless Congress passes a statute otherwise — and Congress didn’t do so here.” The Trump administration sued California , Weber and Logan on Oct. 15 — three months after Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin wrote a letter to Weber alleging that there may be more than 190,000 noncitizens registered to vote in California, and two days after acting Deputy Atty. Gen. Trent McCotter wrote again to Weber and Logan, giving them 48 hours to set aside the ballots for the 20,000 voters on the latest list. Much of the debate since has centered on the origins and evidence in support of that list. California and L.A. County officials have said the list appears to be inaccurate, with Logan’s office saying its review of a subset of about 200 voters found that a substantial portion appeared to have been born in the U.S. — a claim that has been disputed by Homeland Security officials. Elections officials from several other California counties have also raised concerns about the accuracy of smaller lists of voters derived from the 20,000 that were sent to them by Justice Department officials last week, along with a warning that they could face criminal penalties if they tabulate those votes. Officials have said the lists they received contained the names of individuals who did not appear to live in their counties or did not appear to be registered. State officials have pointed to similar lists being rejected as inaccurate elsewhere, including in Nevada. And during Tuesday’s hearing, multiple attorneys for voter advocacy groups — including the NAACP and Mi Familia en Acción — challenged both the origins and the reliability of the Trump administration’s data, and questioned why the Trump administration has so far refused to disclose when and from whom it obtained the purchased California voter roll data it says its analysis is based on. State and county officials have said that complying with the Trump administration’s demands would badly disrupt the election and could disenfranchise legitimate voters who are wrongly included on its inaccurate list. Justice Department officials have defended the list, saying it is composed of 20,000 individuals whom the administration has “high confidence” are not citizens, and that that number represents the “floor” to the issue — while the earlier, 190,000-strong list was the “ceiling” and also included people the administration had suspected but had less confidence were noncitizens. They argued that Carter should immediately bar the state and county from tabulating ballots from the flagged voters until they can prove those voters are citizens — in part because, as soon as cast ballots are received in person or removed from their envelopes, they cannot be resegregated. Essayli has said federal authorities have “overwhelming evidence” to support their claims. At Tuesday’s hearing, he said once federal authorities obtained the purchased voter registration records from the state, they “had to enrich or enhance or add, supplement, information to the voter file, so they took the info that was on there — names, addresses — and they used a database that’s often used by law enforcement, it’s used commercially.” However, in sworn court filings, other administration officials have acknowledged “discrepancies” with some of the records and noted that more recent reviews of the data did show some people on the list appear to have citizenship claims. Essayli told Carter, “We’re never going to stand here and tell you that everything is 100%.” In his ruling Wednesday, Carter also focused in part on the reliability of the list, noting that the process by which the Trump administration compiled it, and the reliability of outside databases to build it, remained unclear and could not be determined to be reliable based on the record before the court — particularly given that administration lists elsewhere have been shown to be unreliable. But Carter also touched on several other weaknesses he saw in the Trump administration’s case — weaknesses that were also hit on by the 9th Circuit panel that rejected the administration’s request Monday. Among them, Carter found that the request violates federal law precluding altering of election rules on the eve of an election. Read more: Judge in L.A. weighs feds' request to block 20,000 California votes with skepticism Carter wrote that prosecutors like Essayli can prosecute individuals who illegally vote — which he called a “clear remedy” to the administration’s concerns about illegal voters casting ballots — but that the administration’s demands to force the state and county to set aside 20,000 ballots at once “would wreak havoc and disrupt the election that is already underway, create a chilling effect on election workers and voters alike, and discount the votes of United States citizens.” “The Executive Branch cannot replace the remedy Congress carefully enacted with its own unlawful and unconstitutional solution instead,” Carter wrote. “Eroded trust in our democracy is irreparable. Once a vote is segregated, lasting harm has occurred. If the Executive can discount votes and threaten an ongoing election due to unproven allegations, then our democracy is in danger,” he wrote. “This Court declines to be a party to such process.” Carter also denounced the Justice Department’s letters to county elections officials threatening them with criminal penalties if they don’t comply with its demands to set the ballots aside — writing that “these threats must stop.” An appeal, if one is filed by the Trump administration, would face a “tough road ahead,” Hasen said. While not guaranteed, the appeal is likely to be taken back up by the same three-judge appellate panel who previously heard — and rejected — the administration’s emergency request to block state officials from counting the ballots. That panel — composed of two appointees of President Trump and one of President Biden — denied the previous request narrowly, ruling 2 to 1 that it did not have jurisdiction over the matter because Carter had not had a chance to rule in the lower court. However, both judges in the majority — Mark J. Bennett, one of the Trump appointees, and Judge Gabriel P. Sanchez, the Biden appointee — wrote separately from the court decision to make clear that they would have denied the administration’s request on the merits too. Among other things, they wrote that the U.S. Constitution gives power over elections to the states and Congress, not the executive branch, and that federal law precludes such voting probes so close to an election. articles.title: 新乳业前三季度净利增长13%，低温奶市场份额继续提升
articles.summary: 乳制品市场延续分化，新乳业依靠低温产品保持增长。 10月29日，新希望乳业股份有限公司披露2026年第三季度报告。 前三季度，公司实现营业收入88.58亿元，同比增长5.03%；归母净利润7.05亿元，同比增长13.23%。 其中，第三季度营收30.45亿元，同比增长4.72%；归母净利润2.40亿元，同比增长6.19%，增速较上半年有所放缓。 支撑增长的核心仍是低温乳品。前三季度，新乳业低温品类收入保持双位数增长，新品收入占比同样维持在双位数水平。 第三方零售监测数据也反映出新乳业在低温市场的竞争力。 马上赢近期发布的《2026Q3乳制品市场回顾》显示，第三季度国内线下低温纯牛奶销售额同比增长17.03%，低温酸奶微增0.18%，常温纯牛奶则继续下滑。 在低温纯牛奶和低温酸奶两个市场，新乳业均位列份额前五，且与君乐宝一起，成为两个品类中仅有的份额同比提升的头部集团。 不过，新乳业与头部竞争对手仍存在规模差距。按2025年整体低温奶市场销售额计算，新乳业市场份额约为9.7%，位列全国第五。 与全国性乳业巨头不同，新乳业通过华西、雪兰、朝日唯品等区域品牌和本地化供应链开展经营。 低温乳品对奶源、冷链运输及终端周转要求较高，区域化布局有助于缩短配送距离，也使公司能够针对不同地区的消费偏好开发产品。 但市场份额提升并不意味着盈利空间同步扩大。 前三季度，新乳业营业成本同比增长6.16%，高于营收增速，整体毛利率约28.71%，同比下降0.76个百分点。 利润增长更多受益于费用端改善。同期销售费用同比下降4.11%，销售费用率降至14.57%。 与此同时，乳制品行业的竞争正在从传统品牌之间，延伸至零售渠道的自有品牌。 近年来，盒马、山姆、奥乐齐等零售商持续扩大自有品牌乳品布局，通过集中采购、定制生产及价格优势争夺消费者。新乳业本身也是部分渠道自有品牌乳品的供应商。 这类合作能够为乳企带来稳定订单，但渠道掌握产品定价、品牌和终端流量，也可能压缩传统乳企自有品牌的溢价空间。 对新乳业而言，如何在扩大低温乳品市场份额的同时，平衡自有品牌经营与渠道代工业务的收益，将成为后续盈利能力的重要考验。 风险提示及免责条款 市场有风险，投资需谨慎。本文不构成个人投资建议，也未考虑到个别用户特殊的投资目标、财务状况或需要。用户应考虑本文中的任何意见、观点或结论是否符合其特定状况。据此投资，责任自负。

articles.summary: 礼来公司凭借旗下减重与糖尿病药物的强劲需求，交出一份远超华尔街预期的三季度成绩单，并再度上调全年展望，进一步巩固其在全球GLP-1药物市场的领导地位。 公司第三季度营收达244亿美元，同比增长39%，超出分析师平均预期的225亿美元；调整后每股收益7.48美元，亦大幅高于预期的5.59美元。受此提振，礼来股价周四早盘上涨3.7%，年内累计涨幅扩大至约20%。 礼来将全年营收指引上调至910亿至920亿美元，高于此前的850亿至870亿美元区间，这是公司今年以来第三次上调全年展望。 与此同时，考虑到近期收购产生的相关费用，公司将调整后每股收益指引小幅下调至35至36美元。 受此提振，礼来股价盘前涨4.3%。 Mounjaro与Zepbound双轮驱动，贡献逾六成营收 三季度业绩的核心推动力来自两款GLP-1明星药物。 糖尿病治疗药物Mounjaro实现营收107.2亿美元，同比增长65%，超出市场预期的99.5亿美元；减重药物Zepbound营收53.5亿美元，较上季度增长8.6%，同样高于预期的50.1亿美元。 两款产品合计占礼来总营收的比例高达66%。 Zepbound的强劲表现部分受益于美国医疗保险政策的重大转变。自今年7月1日起，Medicare首次将减重药物纳入覆盖范围，据礼来介绍，目前约有50万名患者正通过所谓的"Bridge项目"使用Foundayo或Zepbound。据杰富瑞分析师Akash Tewari本周早些时候在研报中估计，该项目有望在年底前为礼来带来约40亿美元的收入贡献。 礼来全球市场总裁Ilya Yuffa上月在摩根士丹利全球医疗健康大会上表示，"Bridge项目在Medicare中的推进，可能是提升药物可及性的最重要单一驱动因素。" 减重口服药Foundayo上市初期表现逊于预期 尽管整体业绩亮眼， 礼来的减重口服药Foundayo表现未达市场预期，成为本季度的一处软肋。 该药三季度营收为1.84亿美元，低于FactSet预期的2.99亿美元，仅略高于其上市首季（二季度）录得的9800万美元。 分析人士指出，Foundayo面临来自诺和诺德旗下减重口服药的竞争压力——后者较Foundayo早数月进入市场，已占据一定先发优势。据杰富瑞数据，礼来目前在美国处方减重药市场的份额约为64%，但减重口服药赛道的竞争格局尚未完全确立。 其他品类药物表现分化：心血管及糖尿病口服药Jardiance营收15.8亿美元，同比大增65%；乳腺癌药物Verzenio营收15.1亿美元，符合预期；传统糖尿病药物Trulicity营收9.04亿美元，同比下滑14%，延续萎缩趋势。 研发管线进展积极，监管获批消息密集 三季度内，礼来在监管层面取得多项进展。美国FDA批准Mounjaro新适应症，用于降低2型糖尿病成人患者的心血管风险；同时批准了每周一次的基础胰岛素Onswik、乳腺癌联合疗法Inluriyo以及用于未经治疗慢性淋巴细胞白血病的Jaypirca扩展适应症。 研发管线方面，礼来披露了多项积极的临床数据：在一项三期头对头试验中，retatrutide在2型糖尿病成人患者中的疗效优于司美格鲁肽2mg；Ebglyss在中重度手足特应性皮炎的三期研究中显示正面结果；EloraTZP在肥胖合并2型糖尿病患者中的二期结果亦为阳性，公司计划于2026年四季度启动三期试验。 本季度研发费用为42亿美元，同比增长21%。此外，公司因收购迷幻药开发商AtaiBeckley及疫苗生物技术公司Curevo，计入了约42亿美元的在研项目研发摊销费用（IPR&D），这也是当季净利润65亿美元低于近期季度水平的主要原因。 风险提示及免责条款 市场有风险，投资需谨慎。本文不构成个人投资建议，也未考虑到个别用户特殊的投资目标、财务状况或需要。用户应考虑本文中的任何意见、观点或结论是否符合其特定状况。据此投资，责任自负。

articles.title: 黄金和美债，谁更避险？
articles.summary: 黄金既是长期储备资产，也是可以迅速变现的金融资产；既承接了避险需求，也承载了趋势交易和杠杆仓位——10月8日后美股下跌，美债避险价值凸显、收益率回落，但黄金却未能获得避险资金青睐的现象，原因即是此。 首先，去杠杆可能引发了跨市场的流动性紧张。 美股下跌、美债利率下行、黄金下跌的场景，在2008年、2020年的极端下跌行情中均有出现。但这一次的不同点在于：第一，美股下跌幅度远不及2008年、2020年；第二，反映市场短期流动性需求的美元指数也并未显著走强。 对于前者，虽然美股没有发生恐慌性暴跌，但几个AI叙事主导的股市共振式下跌，可能还是触发了局部去杠杆，造成杠杆投资者需要抛售资产换取现金，以补充保证金仓位的短期需求。 对于后者，可能与日本央行的干预有关。观察今年2月以来已获确认的日元干预行动（图中为USDJPY汇率，绿色大阴线为BOJ干预当天的美日汇率表现），10月22日当日，市场走势与每次BOJ干预行动发生时的表现相似，这可能是新一轮干预的信号，但证实只能靠事后确认。若BOJ干预压制了美元“原本应该走强”的事实，则进一步确认了黄金下跌的原因是流动性紧张引发的抛售。 在市场流动性压力下，黄金的风险资产属性与黄金矿业股的表现有一定相关性。黄金矿业股过去积累的大涨又会反作用于黄金，加大黄金本身的风险资产属性和价格弹性。过去一个月（9.26-10.27），黄金矿业股ETF（GDX）下跌约12.3%，对比同期的纳斯达克100 ETF（QQQ）下跌约3.9%，现货黄金下跌约6.1%。虽然对通胀的担忧、实际收益率下降和地缘政治风险仍在叙事上支撑黄金，但资金面的抛售对短期价格的影响占据主导。 其次，黄金与美债，各自避的险不同。 买美债，是对冲（美国）经济增长和市场的风险，或者非美经济体的政治风险；换句话说，在美元体系稳定的前提下，美债的对立面是美股。而买黄金，则是对冲美元体系本身的信用风险，比如对AI提升美国生产力的质疑。 市场对AI的分歧，让黄金持续存在对冲价值。如果AI能够持续提高生产率，并将模型收入和企业效率改善转化为真实利润，那么美国的潜在增长和税基可能获得支撑，削弱黄金的相对吸引力。 反过来，如果AI收入增长不足以覆盖资本开支、折旧和融资成本，市场就可能重新评估此前投入的经济回报。一旦这种担忧从企业盈利扩展至金融稳定、财政负担和未来政策应对，黄金对冲美元信用风险的价值便可能上升。 市场目前只是担心AI投资回报不及预期、科技股估值需要调整，尚未怀疑整个AI产业的发展和美国整体融资能力。AI科技类股票的价格在OpenAI、Anthropic披露模型收入增速放缓、CRWV信用风险发酵后下跌，但AI产业的资本支出绝对规模、全球大模型总使用量仍在增加。 对AI科技股的怀疑与对AI产业甚至美元信用的怀疑，是两个不同层次的交易。前者已经发生，并不意味着后者必然同步发生。资金可以卖出科技股、买入美国国债，继续留在美元体系内部。因此，美债比黄金更直接受益。 此外，同期欧洲的经济和政治环境恶化也凸显了美国经济政治体系的相对韧性，压制以买入黄金为代表的“做空美国”交易。 最后，油价与加息的不确定性，仍是黄金的短期约束。 10月FOMC会议美联储维持政策利率不变，但仍有两位委员主张加息25个基点；声明也强调通胀仍然偏高，需要更多信息判断后续政策方向。本次暂停为观察此前加息的效果留出了时间，但黄金面临的实际利率压力尚未解除。 沃什在发布会上指出：近期油价继续上涨，市场利率却有所回落；利率已经影响到科技领域的投资与融资，部分资产信用利差明显走阔，资金配置也更加审慎；整体金融条件“有所收紧”，资金配置更加审慎。这意味着，美联储已观察到利率向科技投资和信用条件的传导，但并未释放更明确的宽松信号。 短期来看，黄金的走势需要观察油价、战争与利率预期的组合。若冲突升级、油价冲高，但加息预期不再上升，且名义利率涨幅低于通胀预期，实际利率便可能回落，为黄金提供支撑。在这一情景下，若黄金仍因去杠杆或流动性导致下跌，就可能进入底部。 长期来看，黄金长期的配置价值仍相对确定，根本支撑是发达国家财政赤字扩张与债务累积对法币信用的持续侵蚀。黄金的配置空间与市场对AI的乐观程度相关：对AI的乐观对应黄金的顶部，对AI的悲观对应黄金的底部。AI收入的能见度越高，黄金的配置空间越被压缩；能见度越低，黄金的配置空间越大。 风险提示 通胀、战争与货币紧缩超预期；跨市场去杠杆超预期；AI投资回报与生产率提振超预期。 本文来源： 宋雪涛 风险提示及免责条款 市场有风险，投资需谨慎。本文不构成个人投资建议，也未考虑到个别用户特殊的投资目标、财务状况或需要。用户应考虑本文中的任何意见、观点或结论是否符合其特定状况。据此投资，责任自负。

articles.title: 牧原前三季度亏损93.19亿元，停建124个猪场应对猪价低谷
articles.summary: 生猪价格持续低迷，牧原股份前三季度由盈转亏。 10月29日，牧原股份发布2026年第三季度报告。前三季度，公司实现营业收入922.00亿元，同比下降17.52%；归母净利润亏损93.19亿元，而去年同期盈利147.79亿元。 其中，第三季度实现营收327.90亿元，同比下降7.18%；归母净利润亏损32.41亿元，较二季度的48.63亿元亏损有所收窄。 养殖成本持续下降，仍然没能抵消猪价下跌的影响。 今年前三季度，牧原累计销售商品猪5873万头。9月份，公司商品猪销量达到642.3万头，同比增长15.24%，但销售均价同比下跌19.57%至10.36元/公斤，单月销售收入反而下降6.01%。 与此同时，牧原生猪养殖完全成本已从年初的12元/公斤，下降至9月份略低于11.5元/公斤。 尽管育种、营养配方和健康管理等环节的效率持续改善，但商品猪销售均价仍低于养殖完全成本。前三季度，公司营业成本达到942.63亿元，超过同期营业收入，毛利率约为-2.24%。 猪价持续低迷，也在改变这家头部养殖企业的经营选择。 过去，规模扩张既能扩大市场份额，也有利于摊薄部分固定成本。但当行业供给充裕、猪价持续低迷，新增养殖产能未必能带来更高利润，反而意味着更多的资金投入和经营压力。 牧原已经开始主动收缩产能。 10月23日，在第十五届李曼中国养猪大会上，牧原股份创始人、终身荣誉董事长秦英林披露，公司已停建124个在建猪场，涉及规划产能1200万头；停产92个猪场，涉及产能670万头。 截至9月末，牧原能繁母猪存栏量已从高峰期的362万头降至297.4万头，减少约64.6万头。 秦英林还透露，如果没有停建上述猪场，牧原原本规划的母猪规模将达到450万头。 “我们自己从调产中受益了。”秦英林坦言，此前市场曾预期今年六七月猪价回升，但最终未能兑现。 除了削减部分产能，公司还在调整生产经营策略。 牧原集团副总经理袁合宾近期表示，公司采取“稳健收缩”策略，将出栏生猪平均体重控制在120公斤以内，不押注短期猪价反弹。 这意味着，在等待行业供需关系改善的同时，牧原开始更加重视产能效率和资金使用，而非单纯追求出栏规模增长。 但收缩养殖规模之后，企业仍然需要寻找新的利润增长空间。 屠宰肉食业务正在成为牧原重点拓展的方向。 今年前三季度，公司累计屠宰生猪2583万头，同比增长34.8%。其中，上半年屠宰肉食业务实现营业收入220.61亿元，同比增长14.04%，并继续保持盈利。 在8月份的业绩交流会上，牧原管理层透露，当前屠宰肉食业务的分割品占比约30%—40%，未来将进一步提升高价值分割品比例。 牧原此前还提出，未来一头猪在养殖端与屠宰端创造的价值增益空间有望超过100元。 不过，这仍是公司对未来经营改善空间的判断，并非已经实现的利润。屠宰肉食业务虽然保持盈利，但相较于养殖业务的庞大体量，目前仍难以扭转集团整体亏损。 现金流同样是牧原在周期底部需要面对的考验。 前三季度，公司经营活动现金流净额为29.83亿元，同比下降89.56%。截至9月末，货币资金达到228.88亿元，较年初增长65.11%，但增长主要来自股票发行募集资金，而非经营活动产生的现金流改善。 从暂停新增猪场建设、调减能繁母猪，到继续降低养殖成本、向下游高价值肉制品延伸，牧原正在调整过去依靠规模扩张的增长路径。 不过，养殖成本下降和屠宰业务发展，都无法完全消除生猪价格波动的影响。 对牧原而言，下一阶段的考验不仅是把猪养得更便宜，还在于能否在不依赖持续扩张养殖规模的情况下，从每头猪身上获得更稳定的利润。 风险提示及免责条款 市场有风险，投资需谨慎。本文不构成个人投资建议，也未考虑到个别用户特殊的投资目标、财务状况或需要。用户应考虑本文中的任何意见、观点或结论是否符合其特定状况。据此投资，责任自负。

articles.title: 中选之后 美国股市可能将遭受巨大压力
articles.summary: 一周后的美国中期选举，华尔街表面上风平浪静，VIX在19附近晃荡，基金经理们嘴里念叨着一个统计数据：1946年以来，中选后12个月标普500从未下跌。像念护身符一样。 但护身符有个前提：以前美股从来没有在席勒CAPE逼近41倍、十年期美债收益率站上5%、AI资本开支占GDP 2%、前十大成分股吃掉指数一半权重的时候，去迎接一次国会易手。 这一次民主党拿下众院的概率超过九成，横扫两院的概率在六成左右。
